prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

If you're not sure about something, just say so.

response.content:
Here's what official CPython sources (PEPs, documentation, and Steering Council statements) say about the performance impact of the free-threaded build.

**Key claims & quotes:**

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Execution Overhead on pyperformance 1.0.6" | CLAIM: PEP 703's original benchmark estimates were ~5‑8% single-threaded and ~7‑8% multi-threaded overhead for the `--disable-gil` build (Intel Skylake: 6%/8%; AMD Zen 3: 5%/7%).

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking." | CLAIM: The overhead primarily comes from biased reference counting and per-object locking, not from memory layout changes.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks... is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it's more like 3%)." | CLAIM: Current CPython free-threaded builds show ~10% single-threaded overhead on Linux/Windows and ~3% on macOS, with active work to reduce it below 10%.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)" | CLAIM: Memory overhead is significant (~15‑20%) and is considered a fundamental trade-off, not a bug to be fully eliminated.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Acceptable performance. The Steering Council mentioned they expected free-threaded Python to be around 10-15% slower... we propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: The Steering Council has set 15% as the maximum acceptable performance penalty for Phase II (official support), and current ~10% overhead meets this target.

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official Python 3.14 documentation reports lower overhead figures (~1‑8%) than PEP 779, suggesting improvements since PEP 779 was written (note: this doc reflects 3.14.5/3.14.7, likely newer data).

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build. There are multiple reasons for this, mostly due to design decisions." | CLAIM: The documentation confirms higher memory usage is expected and by design, though it doesn't give specific percentages (unlike PEP 779).

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "At this point we're expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Steering Council formally accepted PEP 703 with the explicit expectation that free-threaded builds would be 10‑15% slower, and they did not set stricter limits to avoid measurement disputes.

SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code." | CLAIM: The GIL-enabled (default) build must remain unaffected; API/ABI changes needed for free-threading must have negligible cost in the default build.

NO_SOURCE_FOUND: Any official statement on whether free-threaded performance will ever reach parity with the GIL build (all sources acknowledge ongoing work but give no timeline or promise).

**Context & uncertainty:** There's an apparent tension between PEP 779 (~10% current overhead) and the 3.14 docs (~8% on Linux x86-64). This likely reflects either (a) measurement on different hardware/benchmark versions, or (b) improvements since PEP 779's writing. The Steering Council explicitly refused to set hard limits beyond 15% for Phase II, saying solutions that are "currently suboptimal but have room for improvement" are preferable to those "fundamentally problematic for performance improvements going forward."
